When this man, restored by his kinsmen's wealth and care,
had driven out the disease and the bile with neat hellebore,
and come back to himself: "By heaven, you have killed me, friends,
not saved me," he said, "from whom pleasure has thus been wrenched
and the mind's most welcome delusion taken away by force."
No doubt it is profitable to be wise, casting trifles aside,
and to leave play to boys, for whom it is timely,
and not to chase after words to be tuned to Latin strings,
but to learn by heart the rhythms and measures of a true life.
Therefore I say these things to myself, and silently recall:
If no abundance of water could quench your thirst,
you would tell the doctors: dare you confess to no one
that the more you have gained, the more you crave?
If a wound were no easier for the root or herb prescribed,
you would shun the root or herb that did
your healing no good: you had heard that to the man on whom
the gods bestowed wealth, his crooked folly fell away;
and since you are no wiser for being richer,
do you still use the same advisers?
But if riches could make a man prudent,
could make you less greedy and less timid, surely you would blush
if anyone lived on earth more miserly than you.
If a thing is one's own which a man has bought with weights and bronze,
then—if you trust the lawyers—usage too confers ownership of some things;
the field that feeds you is yours, and Orbius' bailiff,
when he harrows the crops that will soon give you grain,
feels you for his master. You pay your money, you get grapes,
chickens, eggs, a jar of wine: thus, indeed, in this way,
you buy the farm little by little—bought, perhaps, for three hundred
thousand sesterces, or even more.
What does it matter whether you live on what you paid for late or long ago?
The buyer of the Aricine and Veientan land once,
eats the greens he bought, though he thinks otherwise; with bought
wood he warms his kettle against the cold night;
yet he calls it all his own, up to where the poplar planted
on the fixed boundaries wards off neighbours' quarrels; as though
anything were one's own, which in the moment of a fleeting hour,
now by prayer, now by price, now by force, now by death at last,
changes its masters and passes into another's rights.
So, since perpetual use is given to none, and heir
follows heir of another as wave overtakes wave,
what use are estates or granaries? What good the Lucanian
pastures added to the Calabrian glades, if Orcus reaps
great with small, not to be entreated by gold?
Gems, marble, ivory, Etruscan figurines, paintings,
silver, robes dyed with Gaetulian purple—
there are men who do not have them, and one who does not care to have them.
Why one of two brothers prefers idleness and play and perfume
to the rich palm-groves of Herod, while the other,
wealthy and restless, from dawn to dusk subdues
his woodland field with flames and iron,
the Genius knows—the companion who governs our natal star,
the god of human nature, mortal in each single head,
changeful of countenance, white and black.
I shall use, and take from my modest heap as much as need
shall ask, nor shall I fear what my heir may judge of me,
that he found no more than I was given; and yet I shall likewise
wish to know how much a frank and cheerful man differs
from a spendthrift, and how much the thrifty differs from the miser.
For it makes a difference whether you scatter your goods as a prodigal,
or neither make outlay unwillingly nor toil to gain more,
but rather, as a boy of old at the festal Quinquatrus,
snatch enjoyment of the brief and welcome time.
Let squalid poverty be far from my house: whether I am borne
in a great ship or a small, I am borne one and the same man.
We are not driven on with swelling sails by a favouring North wind,
yet neither do we drag out our life against opposing South winds;
in strength, talent, looks, virtue, station, estate,
last of the first, and ever ahead of the last.
"You are not greedy: be off." What then? Have the other vices fled
along with that one? Is your breast free of empty
ambition? Free of the fear of death, and of anger?
Dreams, magic terrors, marvels, witches,
night-spectres, and Thessalian portents—do you laugh at them?
Do you count your birthdays with thanks? Do you forgive your friends?
Do you grow gentler and better as old age draws near?
What good does it do you to have one thorn drawn out of many?
If you do not know how to live rightly, give way to those who do.
You have played enough, eaten enough, and drunk enough:
it is time for you to depart, lest, having drunk too freely,
the age that is more becoming in play laugh at you and shove you off.
